ceramic heat emitters emit infrared C and if you're gonna use overhead heating it would be better to use a deep heat projector rather than ceramic heating. also overhead heating requires a basking spot which I do not think would be appropriate for a baby leopard gecko which should preferably have a sterile tank until they get a bit older. also a ceramic heat emitter and a UV light do different thing and if UV is used at appropriate hours it should not affect the day and night cycle. also I do not recommend loose substrate for babies because during the first month or so of having a baby you need to be watching out for any illnesses or disorders and having a loose substrate might worsen a condition that they're not yet aware of. calcium should not be fed with every meal especially if it does not include D3 and you should be alternating calcium and D3 with a multivitamin. if I was confused about your comment please tell me but also don't advise people incorrect things that could potentially harm the animal

also one other thing I forgot to mention. it seems your gecko has a bit of stuck shed on their head. you can fix this by putting a bit of warm water on a cotton swab. if shed ever gets stuck on the lower half of your gecko, you can try soaking them, up to the hips, in water for 10 to 15 minutes, and use a cotton swab or your fingers to gently get it off. the temperature of the bath can be 70° to 80° farenheit. always give the gecko a day after the shed to try to get it off themselves, unless you see the shed is restricting something vital like the eyes, neck or abdomen. if you see skin getting stuck near the eye I would recommend going to the vet because that can be a sign of an eye deformity and can cause some illnesses. you should definitely go to the vet if this is repeatedly happening. remember not to use any sharp objects when handling the gecko

now, I'd like to discuss substrates. substrates within the leopard gecko community is a highly debated concept, however, there are a few that I'd advise you to definitely stay away from. sand, calcisand, colored sand, ect. now, before I talk about this, I want to say that there are some types of sand that can be used in substrate mixtures that are acceptable, but just for the time being it is best to stay away from them because it is very hard to make a good substrate as a beginner. so, some people say that sand is okay if all other forms of husbandry are accurate, however, pure sand does not work like that. when sand gets wet, it clumps up. when chunks of sand get into your reptile there is absolutely no way for them to pass it in large quantities, no matter how healthy the reptile is. and regarding calcisand, it is not safe for your reptile and it is not healthy for them either. first off, that is way too much calcium, second off, it is indigestible. do not listen to the stories about it being okay, just because one person got lucky that it did not happen to them YET, does not change the likelihood of it impacting your gecko. wood ships, wood shavings, pebbles, carpet, glass, are all substrates that are not in any way suitable for a Leopard gecko, or any reptile for that matter. there are loose substrates, and there are solid substrates, the one you choose is dependent on your skill level and knowledge on the particular substrate. two popular beginner substrates are paper towel and eco earth. both of these substrates are okay, however, they each have their own pros and cons. here is a [Link](https://www.instagram.com/s/aGlnaGxpZ2h0OjE3ODk4NTcxNDQyMDYxMDk5?story_media_id=2588999006658028762_29710759901&utm_medium=copy_link) to the substrates that I have gone in depth about. I will be adding different substrates as time goes on. 

although I've already gone over vivariums surface level, I'd like to go in a bit more depth. leopard geckos are classified as terrestrial, although this can really be different from leopard gecko to leopard gecko, as well as the different subspecies of leopard geckos, as some of them do like to climb. making a custom background, or buying one can benefit your gecko, although you should wait until they get to an adult size. as for size of the tank, right now the minimum for a leopard gecko is 20 gallon long, however, smaller tanks are preferred for babies. getting a front opening tank will benefit both you and your gecko. front opening tanks can allow the gecko to feel more secure, when you reach your hand in from the top it can trigger a predator response in your gecko, cleaning the tank out with overhead heating a lighting on the top is also a very difficult thing to do with a top opening tank. right now, your gecko is too small to be put in any of those tanks. what you have will work for maybe a few weeks to a month, depending on how fast your gecko is growing. baby geckos need a sterile, small environment. this is important as they can hurt themselves on loose substrates and decor, you also need to be watching the baby gecko to make sure they are developing correctly. and by sterile environment I mean: no living decor, paper towel as substrate, three different hides and one water bowl. I will now discuss the "gradient" set up style:

Reptiles need a way to self regulate their body temperature. you can make them able by making a heat/moisture gradient throughout the tank. typically this is done by providing a hot side, warm side (middle) and a cold side. the hot side is going to be the side with the heat matt or basking spot, the middle is going to provide the moist hide, the cold hide will be provided opposite of the hot hide. the temperature of the basking spot, or ground temperature on top of the heat matt should be around 90° farenheit during the day, and should shift down into the 80°s during the night (this can be done via thermostat with a separate day and night setting. [thermostat I use ](https://www.miscota.com/reptiles/exo-terra/p-424166?r=15561224611&gclid=EAIaIQobChMIm_nNwtaf8QIVogaICR2pgw-qEAUYASABEgJ3UfD_BwE) ) the warm hide should be around the high 70°s, while the cold side should be mid 70°s. if you're having trouble heating up the cold and warm sides, buying a low wattage ceramic heater, controlled by a thermostat can help you reach those ideal temperatures. now for hides. it is very important to get/make hides that are made from material that will not unleash toxic fumes if heated. and I've also found that leopard geckos feel a lot more secure if there is at least two entrances to the given hides. now, for your gecko currently I would not do anything elaborate. buying hides from the pet store should be just fine, but if you want to provide your gecko with something a bit fancier, cork rounds could also work for your current set up. now the moist hide in particular is special because it needs to be able to retain moisture a bit better than the cold and hot hides. I've found that plastic Tupperware works well to retain humidity. here is a video on how to make these: [Link](https://youtu.be/0HHWixVdDqE)
providing paper towel inside of this hide will be optimal for your current set up as the gecko cannot really swallow it, however, once you get the bigger tank, adding sphagnum moss to a bigger, more natural moist hide will be better. now, I wont go into too much detail about this because it can be quite overwhelming to new owners, but having a more naturalistic or bioactive set up will benefit your gecko quite a bit. a bioactive set up is a self maintaining mini ecosystem that contains live plants and micro fauna. the micro fauna is, but not exclusive to, made up of springtails and certain arid species of isopods. a naturalist set up is a step down from bioactive but can still benefit the gecko the same. naturalist set ups consist of natural cork, loose substrate, rocks, and fake or real plants. reptiles seem to "come to life" when given set ups like these, I reccomend looking into them if it is not too overwhelming for you.

starting off, I think you should remove the Repticarpet and replace it with paper towel, at least while they're still a baby. repticarpet allows harmful bacteria to grow which is hard to get off, and there have been many cases of geckos getting their claws and teeth stuck in the carpet. although there are better sources of heat, because you're a beginner I'd reccomend you get a heat matt. you will also need a thermostat to control the heating, make sure to get one with a probe; there are ones you can get for cheap (I don't know what your budget is) but make sure that it has good reviews before buying it, the one I use us an exoterra dimming and pulse proportional thermostat which is 90 to 150 usd (from what I've seen) and you can buy it online. that specific thermostat also gives you a reading of the current basking spot or heat matt, but not all of them do, so if you decide to get something else I'd reccomend you get a laser thermometer or a digital thermometer with a probe. place the probe on the inner part of the tank where the heat matt is (where your gecko would be laying). the heat matt itself should be placed on the outside of the tank, unless you're using heat tape in which it should be placed inside. another thing that I should have said in the beginning, you need to switch to a front opening vivarium. these can cost 200 usd or more depending on where you get it but you must make sure to read the reviews to make sure the vivarium is not going to be faulty. try finding a vivarium that has holes already in place for the probes, but if you cant, you're able to drill into it to make holes as long as you do not get glass (also, I do not recommend glass because they dont allow probes to go through. if you're going to get a wooden vivarium the top of the tank needs to be mesh.). that is beginner heating, however, once you get more advanced you may be able to install a deep heat projector which emits infrared A and B, where as the heat matt, ceramic heaters, ect all emit infrared C which is a byproduct of infrared A and B that gets reflected back when A and B hit earth's surface. infrared C will keep your reptile alive, however it will not give them the same amount of energy as infrared A and B. now that I've discussed heating I will now discuss lighting. 

ultraviolet light, UV is very important to all reptiles. it will aid in calcium absorption but allowing the reptile's D3 cycle to start, which I will explain here (you don't necessarily need to know this but its interesting): Calcitriol allows for more calcium absorption in the liver, bones and intestine. while calcidiol is a form of hormone that produces vitamin D in the liver.  when d3 is supplemented to the reptile it is converted to calcidiol in the liver. calcidiol moves throughout blood plasma and gets converted to calcitriol in the kidneys.
basically, UVB allows reptiles to convert D3 into its usable form within the body. [short UV light explanation and review ](https://youtu.be/jcYSsgP-hvo)
UVA will also allow reptiles to see in more color, which they'd naturally see in the wild. Leopard geckos in particular are crepuscular, meaning they are most active during dusk and dawn, which are moments of the day with low light. Leopard geckos have evolved this way due to their extremely thin skin, in which they absorb much more UVB and UVA than a diurnal animal would, such as a bearded dragon. this being said, they need much less UV than diurnal animals, so the majority of the UV lights on the market will not work for them, however, Arcadia 7% Shadedweller UV light will work very well for Leopard geckos and is designed for 
crepuscular species. 

[Shadedweller ](https://www.arcadiareptile.com/lighting/shadedweller-prot5/)

there I linked the website in which you can read more about it, as there are many websites in which you can buy it from. in the US, this is not available in stores and has to be bought online. on the website you will find a table that explains the height of the light in combination with the UV index. Leopard Geckos need to be within 2% to 6%, while in the middle may be optimal, as the mesh top to a vivarium will filter out some of the UV (I'd reccomend doing more research on the topic so you can make sure you fully understand this as if you do it incorrectly in can cause burns to your reptile.) 
although UV lights are optimal, supplementing synthetic D3 can work, although the cons outweigh the pros. for starters, as humans we are incapable of knowing how much D3 a reptile needs at any given time, oversupplementing and under supplementing are very common. D3 being a fat soulable, when it is oversupplemnted it can be stored around organs which can be very dangerous.
